PROPERTY FROM A PRESTIGIOUS PRIVATE COLLECTION, SYDNEYDAVID HOCKNEY (1937-2026)
Cataract Hotel Aswan 
signed with the artist's initials, titled and dated 'Cataract Hotel Aswan DH 78' (lower right)
coloured pencil on paper 
43.5 x 35.5cm (17 1/8 x 14in).
Executed in 1978

Provenance
Knoedler Gallery, London 
Anon. sale, Sotheby's, New York, 20 February 1987, lot 124 
Dennis Hotz Fine Art, South Africa 
Private Collection, Sydney (acquired from the above in 1987)

David Hockney's Cataract Hotel Aswan is a vivid testament to the artist's enduring fascination with Egypt and with the possibilities of drawing as a means of translating visual experience into colour, line and memory. Executed in 1978, fifteen years after his first visit to the country, the work belongs to a small but significant group of drawings made during Hockney's return to Egypt with his close friends Peter Schlesinger and Joe McDonald. Yet rather than depicting one of the ancient monuments for which the country is renowned, Hockney turns his attention to the interior of the historic Old Cataract Hotel. Through the immediacy of coloured pencil, an architectural interior becomes an intensely personal study of light, space and perception.

The Old Cataract Hotel, situated on the banks of the Nile in Aswan, had opened in 1900 and quickly established itself as an important destination for travellers on the river. Its commanding position and distinctive architecture contributed to its status as one of Aswan's defining landmarks. For Hockney, however, the hotel provided more than a picturesque subject. Returning to Egypt after an absence of fifteen years, he was revisiting a landscape already embedded within his visual memory. The decision to record the interior of the hotel is therefore particularly revealing instead of seeking the monumental or the spectacular, Hockney finds visual richness in an inhabited, everyday space.

The composition is immediately animated by colour. Executed entirely in coloured pencil, the drawing is dominated by vivid reds, pinks and yellows, punctuated by cooler blues, ochres and pale greens. At its centre, a boldly outlined red chair acts as a powerful visual anchor. Its sweeping contours and emphatic colour distinguish it from the more loosely rendered elements around it, drawing the eye into the space while giving the composition a sense of rhythm. The chair is at once an ordinary piece of furniture and an almost abstract form, demonstrating Hockney's ability to discover formal interest in the most familiar of subjects.

Around this focal point, the architecture establishes a contrasting sense of order. Strong verticals and the geometric divisions of the windows provide a rigorous framework, while the surrounding interior is described through quicker, more economical marks. Hockney does not attempt to render every detail with equal precision; instead, he allows certain areas to remain open and suggestive. The result is a compelling tension between the solidity of the architecture and the freedom of the artist's hand. The building provides structure, but within that structure the drawing remains fluid and alive.

This balance is fundamental to the character of the work. Hockney's lines vary from delicate, rapidly drawn marks to more emphatic passages in which form is asserted through colour and contour. The coloured pencil allows him to work with extraordinary immediacy, building saturated areas of pigment while retaining the freshness of the individual stroke. Rather than functioning simply as a descriptive medium, colour becomes a means of interpreting the space. The heightened reds and pinks, set against cooler passages, intensify the sensation of light and give the interior an atmosphere that is recognisably observed yet unmistakably transformed through the artist's perception.

The importance of the work also lies in this distinction between recording and interpretation. Hockney's second journey to Egypt followed almost a year of concentrated work on his stage designs for Mozart's The Magic Flute at Glyndebourne. His return to the country brought him back into direct contact with a landscape and culture that had first made a strong impression on him in 1963. In Cataract Hotel Aswan, however, memory does not result in a nostalgic reconstruction. Instead, it becomes a catalyst for renewed looking. The familiar is re-encountered and reorganised through the immediacy of drawing
.
This makes the present work particularly revealing within Hockney's broader practice. Perhaps best known for his pools, portraits and California landscapes, Hockney has consistently explored the relationship between perception and representation, questioning how an image can convey not simply what is seen but the experience of seeing. Cataract Hotel Aswan demonstrates this interest on an intimate scale. Its subject is precisely located, yet its vivid colour, abbreviated marks and carefully balanced geometry transform the particular into something more expansive: an exploration of how space, light and memory can be held within a single sheet of paper.

Ultimately, Cataract Hotel Aswan is a testament to Hockney's ability to make the familiar appear newly discovered. The particularity of the setting gives way to something more universal: an image of the moment in which looking becomes experience, and observation becomes memory. In this sense, the drawing transcends its subject, capturing not simply a place, but the fleeting sensation of seeing it anew.

PROPERTY FROM A DISTINGUISHED PRIVATE COLLECTION, ITALYFRANK AUERBACH (1931-2024)
Untitled 
signed and dated 'Auerbach 1954' (lower left of the reverse)
charcoal and pastel on paper, double sided
46.5 x 48cm (18 3/8 x 18 7/8in).
Executed in 1954

Provenance
Marlborough Fine Art Ltd., London
Angela Flowers, London 
Private Collection (acquired from the above circa 1975); their sale, Sotheby's, London, 24 June 2004, lot 243
Austin/Desmond Fine Art, London
Acquired from the above by the present owner circa 2005

Executed in 1954, Untitled belongs to a pivotal moment in Frank Auerbach's early career, when drawing became a means of testing the limits of observation, material and representation. Working from a small group of recurring sitters and familiar London subjects, Auerbach developed images through prolonged engagement rather than swift description. In the present work, the seated figure emerges from dense, interlocking passages of charcoal and pastel, its form suspended between recognition and dissolution. Rather than being defined by a continuous contour, the body is gradually assembled through the accumulation of marks, allowing figure and surrounding space to remain in a state of productive tension.

What makes the present work particularly remarkable, however, is that this process extends across both sides of the sheet. The double-sided construction offers an unusually intimate insight into Auerbach's method: the paper itself becomes a record of looking, reconsideration and revision. The verso is not simply a hidden reverse, but an integral component of the work, expanding the act of drawing beyond the conventional boundaries of a single picture plane. Both surfaces preserve the artist's engagement with the subject, making the physical support inseparable from the image it carries.

This conception of drawing was fundamental to Auerbach's practice. His early charcoal works developed through prolonged sittings, during which the artist repeatedly altered and rebuilt the image in pursuit of what he understood as the sitter's presence. Such sustained revision is palpable here. Rather than functioning as a transparent means of description, charcoal becomes the substance from which the figure is brought into focus, with each addition, erasure and reworking contributing to the final image. The resulting surface records the passage of time as much as the appearance of the sitter.

The seated nude was an important subject within Auerbach's development during the 1950s, providing a demanding framework through which to explore the possibilities of figurative drawing. Here, the body is barely contained by conventional contours. Limbs and torso appear to gather from the surrounding darkness, while repeated strokes alternately define and obscure the anatomy. The density of the charcoal gives the figure an almost sculptural weight, yet its edges remain unstable. Presence is therefore achieved not through descriptive precision, but through the accumulation of material.

In this respect, Untitled exemplifies Auerbach's position within the post-war British figurative tradition and, more specifically, the group of artists later associated with the 'School of London'. Alongside contemporaries including Lucian Freud and Leon Kossoff, Auerbach remained committed to the human figure at a moment when abstraction dominated much of the international art world. These artists shared an interest in sustained observation and the expressive potential of the figure, while developing markedly individual approaches to its representation. For Auerbach, this meant pushing figurative drawing towards a point where description and materiality become inseparable. Rather than seeking clarity or completeness, he made visible the uncertainty inherent in sustained observation, allowing the struggle to arrive at an image to become part of the image itself.

The present work is particularly significant in relation to Auerbach's first solo exhibition at the Beaux Arts Gallery in London in 1956. Held only two years after its execution, the exhibition marked an important early presentation of his intensely worked paintings and drawings. Untitled therefore belongs to a formative period in which the methods that would underpin Auerbach's mature practice were already clearly established: the recurring sitter, the prolonged encounter, the accumulation of material and the continual negotiation between presence and abstraction.

Ultimately, the importance of Untitled lies not simply in its depiction of the human figure, but in the way the work makes the process of seeing tangible. Its unusual double-sided construction gives physical form to Auerbach's continual search for the image, while the densely worked surface preserves the evidence of that search. Across both faces of the sheet, drawing becomes an act of discovery: the figure is not merely observed but gradually brought into being through the sustained encounter between artist, sitter and material.

PROPERTY FROM A PRESTIGIOUS PRIVATE COLLECTION, SYDNEYFERNANDO BOTERO (1932-2023)
Lovers 
incised with the artist's signature, number and foundry mark 'Botero 3/9' (on the base)
bronze
23.5 x 43 x 28.4cm (9 1/4 x 16 7/8 x 11 1/8in).
Executed in 1985, this work is number 3 from an edition of 9

Provenance
Dennis Hotz Fine Art, South Africa 
Private Collection, Sydney (acquired from the above in 1988)

At once intimate in subject and commanding in form, Lovers belongs to a distinguished group of sculptures in which Fernando Botero transformed the human embrace into a study of physical presence and emotional connection. The reclining couple are presented not as individual portraits but as an inseparable sculptural unit, their bodies folding into one another in a configuration that is both tender and formally assured. Botero turns a private gesture of affection into an exploration of balance, rhythm and the sensual possibilities of bronze. Although relatively compact in scale, the work possesses an expansive presence, its rounded forms extending beyond the confines of the rectangular base and establishing an immediate sense of abundance.

The embracing couple occupy an important place within Botero's wider practice, appearing across painting, drawing and sculpture as recurring images of intimacy, companionship and desire. Such subjects allowed the artist to approach the human figure through physical proximity rather than individual identity, making the relationship between bodies itself the principal focus. In the present work, this anonymity is especially significant: the features are reduced to essential indications, while the distinct identities of the two figures are subordinated to the unity of their embrace. Rather than simply depicting affection, Botero makes contact the organising principle of the sculpture, binding two bodies into a single continuous form.

This sense of unity is further developed through the horizontal configuration, which allows the figures to occupy space through a succession of overlapping curves. Limbs, torsos and heads form a continuous sequence of rounded contours, with the body of one figure appearing to support and echo that of the other. Repetition and variation create a quiet visual rhythm, while the rectangular base introduces a contrasting geometric stability beneath the organic forms. The tension between these elements gives the sculpture its particular character: the embrace appears spontaneous and intimate, yet every relationship between mass, contour and support has been carefully resolved.

Within this carefully balanced structure, Botero's characteristic manipulation of proportion takes on a distinctly human significance. The figures are enlarged and simplified, but the exaggeration is tempered by the tenderness of their pose. Shoulders press together, limbs overlap and the generous curves of the bodies seem almost to merge, shifting attention away from anatomical description towards the sensation of physical closeness. Their anonymity allows the embrace to assume a universal quality, while the exaggerated volumes give emotional connection a tangible physical form.

The interdependence of the figures also reflects Botero's longstanding interest in the expressive possibilities of volume. His broad, simplified contours lend the human form an almost architectural clarity, yet here that formal language is softened by the way one body flows into the next. The eye moves continuously across the sculpture, following the curves of the embrace and observing how each form supports, echoes or interrupts another. Meaning consequently emerges not from either figure in isolation, but from the subtle relationships established between them, making the work a particularly concentrated expression of Botero's sculptural language.

The tactile quality of these forms is heightened by the use of bronze, whose dark patina allows light to travel gradually across the rounded surfaces. Highlights gather along the shoulders, knees and faces before receding into the deeper passages between the intertwined bodies, creating a subtle contrast between illumination and shadow. This changing surface reinforces the apparent softness of the modelling while simultaneously asserting the solidity of the material. As the viewer moves around the work, new overlaps and intervals emerge, allowing the intimacy of the subject to be experienced through the changing spatial relationships of the sculpture.
Botero's mature engagement with sculpture provided an especially powerful medium for this investigation of closeness. The physicality of bronze gives weight and permanence to a gesture that is inherently fleeting, while the compact arrangement concentrates the figures into a remarkably unified form. The sculpture consequently occupies an intriguing position between figuration and abstraction: the subject remains immediately recognisable, yet its emotional force depends upon the reduction of the bodies to essential masses, curves and points of contact. The familiar image of two lovers is thereby transformed into an investigation of how sculpture can communicate intimacy through form itself.

It is this union of emotional immediacy and formal discipline that gives Lovers its distinctive power. Botero avoids sentimentality by stripping the figures of individual character, yet the softness of their modelling and the closeness of their pose preserve an unmistakable sense of human warmth. The horizontal configuration, exaggerated proportions and enveloping curves allow a simple subject to sustain considerable formal complexity, revealing how deeply Botero's sculptural language is rooted in the expressive potential of the human body.

Lovers ultimately demonstrates Botero's ability to make intimacy monumental without sacrificing its tenderness. Two anonymous figures become a single sculptural presence, their intertwined bodies creating a continuous language of curves, weight and contact. In the balance between affection and abstraction, softness and solidity, Botero transforms the simplest of human gestures - the embrace - into an enduring meditation on the physical and emotional possibilities of sculpture.

LEON KOSSOFF (1926-2019)
Portrait of ChaÃ¯m 
oil on board
26.5 x 31.5cm (10 3/8 x 12 3/8in).
Painted in 1988

Provenance 
Collection of the artist, UK
Private Collection, London
Gift from the above to the present owner

Exhibited
Hastings, Hastings Contemporary, Soutine | Kossoff, 1 April - 24 September 2023 (illustrated p. 102)

Literature
Andrea Rose, Leon Kossoff Catalogue Raisonné of the Oil Paintings, London, 2021, no. 365 (illustrated p. 439)

For Leon Kossoff, painting was an act of sustained attention. His subjects were never simply transcribed from observation; rather, they were apprehended through a continual process of looking, painting, erasure and renewal. Paint accumulates, is scraped away and rebuilt, until the image seems to exist somewhere between likeness and memory. The resulting surfaces bear the physical record of this prolonged engagement, their dense impasto giving material form to both the sitter and the artist's experience of looking at him. Nowhere is this more intimate than in Kossoff's portraits of his family. Freed from the distance traditionally associated with portraiture, these works register not merely appearance but the changing presence of those whom the artist knew most closely. In Portrait of Chaïm, 1988, this deeply personal mode of enquiry is concentrated upon his brother, Chaim, who became one of the defining subjects of Kossoff's later work.

Chaim assumed particular prominence following the death of their father in 1983, after which Kossoff began to draw and paint his brother with increasing frequency. Drawing remained fundamental to this process. For Kossoff, it was not simply preparatory but a means of apprehending the sitter directly, enabling him to register something beyond physiognomy: temperament, gesture and the elusive quality of a person's presence. Paul Moorhouse observed that these studies revealed a 'rapid, almost immediate sympathy with the subject', resulting in some of Kossoff's most successful figure studies (Paul Moorhouse, Leon Kossoff, Tate Gallery, London, 1996, p. 33). That sympathy is palpable here. Chaim sits quietly, his head inclined and shoulders relaxed, his pose unselfconscious rather than formally composed. There is a remarkable economy to the gesture, yet from the densely worked surface emerges an image of considerable psychological warmth. The portrait feels less like a declaration of identity than an intimate act of recognition.

Kossoff's return to Chaim was central to the nature of this recognition. The Metropolitan Museum of Art holds Portrait of Chaim I, in which the sitter appears to occupy the same red chair as in the present work. Such recurrence was intrinsic to Kossoff's practice. He repeatedly returned to the people and places he knew best, not in pursuit of a definitive likeness but because each encounter offered the possibility of seeing anew. Repetition thus became a means of measuring change: the subtle alteration of a face, the shifting weight of a body, the accumulated signs of time. In the portraits of his family, this sustained attention acquires particular poignancy, as painting becomes a way of holding in view those whose lives were unfolding alongside his own.

The intimacy of Portrait of Chaïm, is inseparable from its physical construction. Kossoff has subjected the board to an extraordinary accumulation of paint, building the image through ridges, folds and sinuous passages of impasto. The surface is emphatically material, yet it never becomes inert. Light blue and red animate the predominantly pale ground, their accents moving across the composition with a force that seems at odds with the sitter's stillness. Rather than enclosing the figure within a stable contour, Kossoff allows him to emerge from a continuous field of colour and gesture. The paint does not describe Chaim so much as generate his presence.

This tension between permanence and transience lay at the heart of Kossoff's mature practice. He was fascinated by the paradox that paint could endure while the subject before him could not. His characteristic method of scraping back and rebuilding the surface made this paradox tangible. Earlier passages remain partially buried beneath subsequent applications, so that the final image contains the memory of its own making. The act of destruction becomes inseparable from creation. In Portrait of Chaïm, the accumulation of these successive states gives the painting an unusual temporal depth: one senses not a single sitting captured in paint, but a history of looking compressed into a single image.

Kossoff's understanding of paint as a vehicle for such direct experience was profoundly shaped by his discovery of Chaïm Soutine in the early 1950s. Soutine offered him a model for an art in which the observed world could be transformed without relinquishing its immediacy. The significance of that encounter was made explicit by Soutine | Kossoff at Hastings Contemporary in 2023, the first museum exhibition devoted to the artistic relationship between the two painters. Bringing together portraiture and landscape, the exhibition illuminated the affinities between their approaches to colour, gesture and the material substance of paint.

Yet In Portrait of Chaïm, also reveals how profoundly personal Kossoff's response to this inheritance became. Where Soutine's subjects could appear charged with an almost volatile intensity, Kossoff's encounter with his brother is quieter, grounded in familiarity and affection. The surface may be turbulent, but the emotional register is one of profound stillness. This distinction is important: Kossoff's impasto is not an expressive veil placed between the viewer and the sitter, but the very means through which intimacy is conveyed.

The result is a portrait of unusual concentration. Chaim's quiet pose is held within a surface that records the relentless activity of the artist's hand; stillness and movement, permanence and transience, recognition and discovery are brought into productive tension. Through the physical substance of paint, Kossoff makes visible the duration of looking and, with it, the depth of his relationship to his subject. In Portrait of Chaïm, is therefore more than a portrait of a brother. It is a meditation on the act of seeing someone known intimately, and on painting's capacity to preserve, however provisionally, the fleeting experience of another human presence.

oil on panel
23.8 x 42.5cm (9 3/8 x 16 3/4in).
Painted in 1884

Provenance
Hippolyte Camp Collection, Marseille (acquired directly from the artist).
Private collection, France.
Dennis Hotz Fine Art, South Africa.
Private collection, Sydney (acquired from the above on 17 September 1987).

Exhibited
Paris, Galerie Daniel Malingue, Maîtres Impressionnistes et Modernes, 7 November - 22 December 1986, no. 3.
Sandton, Dennis Hotz Fine Art, Exhibition of International 19th & 20th Century Impressionist, Modern Paintings, Sculptures and Lithographs, 22 February - 12 March 1988.

Literature
R. Schmit, Eugène Boudin, 1824-1898, Vol. II, Paris, 1973, no. 1868 (illustrated p. 220).

By the 1880s, Trouville had become one of the most recognisable subjects of Eugène Boudin's repertoire. Yet, this repeated return to the fashionable Normandy resort was never simply an exercise in picturesque repetition. The present work, Trouville, Scène de Plage, painted in 1884, is a masterful example of the artist's exploration of the beach as a theatre of modern life.

Boudin first visited Trouville in the early 1860s, when the small fishing town was rapidly becoming a fashionable resort. The development of neighbouring Deauville (where Boudin acquired a house the year the present work was painted), together with the arrival of the railway, transformed the Normandy coast into a seasonal destination for affluent Parisian society. Boudin immediately recognised the artistic possibilities of this new public. His beach scenes offered an alternative to the grand historical and picturesque conventions of contemporary landscape painting: here was a landscape inhabited by the people of his own time. As he wrote in 1868, he had been praised for 'daring to include the things and people of [his] own time in [his] pictures' and asked, 'don't these bourgeois, who stroll on the jetty towards the sunset, have the right to be fixed on canvas, to be brought into the light?' (E. Boudin quoted in V. Hamilton, Boudin at Trouville, exh. cat., Glasgow and London, 1992, p. 20).

It was precisely this social dimension that distinguished Boudin's beaches from conventional marine painting. As Jean Selz observed: 'What fascinated Boudin at Trouville and Deauville was not so much the sea and the ships but the groups of people sitting on the sand or strolling along the beach: fine ladies in crinolines twirling their parasols, pompous gentlemen in top hats, children and little dogs playing on the sand. In the harmony of the colours of the elegant clothes he found a contrast to the delicacy of the skies.' (J. Selz, E. Boudin, New York, 1982, p. 57.)

Selz's observation is particularly relevant to the present work. Boudin arranges his figures in a compressed, frieze-like band, their individual identities dissolved into posture, costume and colour. A brilliant red parasol and a flash of blue punctuate the otherwise harmonious silvery-brown palette, while a seated woman at the right, apparently absorbed in reading, introduces a moment of quiet introspection amid the collective spectacle. The contrast is subtle but telling: the beach is a place of public leisure and sociability, yet also permits moments of private absorption. Faces are scarcely described; instead, Boudin captures the collective choreography of leisure. The beach becomes a place not merely to bathe, but to see and be seen.

The term 'crinoline paintings', now conventionally applied to Boudin's celebrated beach scenes, refers to the fashionable hoop skirts worn by the women who populate his pictures of the 1860s. Nine of the eleven works he exhibited at the Paris Salon between 1864 and 1869 depicted Trouville beaches or jetties, establishing the subject as central to his early reputation. Yet by 1884 the fashion itself had changed, and so had Boudin's treatment of the motif. In the earlier pictures, figures tend to form a distant horizontal band beneath enormous expanses of sky; in the small panels of the 1870s and 1880s they are brought much closer to the viewer, as though encountered at eye level while walking along the strand. The fashionable crowd is consequently no longer simply an accessory to the landscape: it becomes the principal subject.

The immediacy of the present panel is inseparable from Boudin's practice of working from nature. He urged himself in his notebooks: 'Beaches. Produce them from nature as far as is possible.' (E. Boudin quoted in G. Cahen, Eugène Boudin, Sa Vie et son Oeuvre, Paris, 1900, p. 183). Small panels offered a practical support for this direct engagement with the motif. In the present work, this connection with plein air painting is perhaps materially preserved with possible traces of grains of sand embedded in the paint layer, therefore giving us compelling evidence that the picture was at least partly painted sur le motif. The rapidly applied strokes of the figures, the abbreviated parasols and the loose horizontal touches in the sand retain the freshness of an observed moment. Boudin himself recognised the particular force of such direct painting, writing that 'Everything that is painted directly and on the spot has always a strength, a power, a vivacity of touch which one cannot recover in the studio.' (E. Boudin quoted in V. Hamilton, Op. cit., p. 16).

A particularly illuminating comparison is Claude Monet's Sur la plage à Trouville of 1870, now in The National Gallery, London. The two artists worked alongside one another at Trouville that summer, with Boudin's practice of painting directly from nature proving formative for the younger Monet. Indeed, The National Gallery records grains of sand embedded in Monet's wet paint, and the visual appearance of the surface of Trouville, Scène de Plage resembles Monet's painting. Yet the influence can also be seen in reverse: by 1884, Boudin's increasingly abbreviated handling and intimate treatment of the crowd reflect a pictorial language that Monet and the Impressionists had helped to develop. Monet's cropped, close-up composition in Sur la plage à Trouville therefore offers an intriguing counterpart to Boudin's social frieze, suggesting a dialogue between master and pupil that had become reciprocal: Boudin taught Monet to paint outside the studio and in return, Boudin would later learn from Monet and the Impressionists how to get closer to the subjects, painting them with the immediacy of modern life.

Boudin's importance to Impressionism therefore lies partly in this direct engagement with the motif. Sixteen years Monet's senior, he became the younger artist's mentor in Le Havre, encouraging him to work outdoors and to attend closely to light, sky and atmosphere. Monet later acknowledged his debt in unequivocal terms: 'I owe everything to Boudin and I attribute my success to him.' (C. Monet quoted in R. Kendall, Monet by Himself, London, 1992, p. 181). 

By 1884, Boudin had spent more than two decades returning to Trouville, and the connection had become deeply personal. Trouville, Scène de Plage belongs to both the culmination of this lifelong subject and to the mature phase of his art. The fashionable crowd that had first captivated him in the age of the crinoline remains, but is now rendered with greater economy and freedom, in this masterful example of the artist's exploration of the beach as a theatre of modern life.

Provenance

Exhibited
Paris, Galerie Durand-Ruel, Berthe Morisot (Madame Eugène Manet), 5 – 23 March 1896, no. 212.
Paris, Galerie Bernheim-Jeune, Cent oeuvres de Berthe Morisot, 7 – 22 November 1919, no. 82 (titled 'Paysage à Mézy' and dated 1890).
Paris, Galerie Durand-Ruel, Exposition Berthe Morisot, 1841-1895, Pastels - Aquarelles - Dessins, 9 - 30 April 1948, no. 51 (dated 1890).
Washington, D.C., National Gallery of Art, Berthe Morisot, Impressionist, 6 September – 29 November 1987, no. 85 (later travelled to Fort Worth and South Hadley).

Literature
M.-L. Bataille & G. Wildenstein, Berthe Morisot, Catalogue des peintures, pastels et aquarelles, Paris, 1961, no. 570 (illustrated fig. 564).

'To name an object is to suppress three-quarters of the enjoyment to be found in the poem... suggestion, that is the dream.' (S. Mallarmé, Enquête sur l'évolution littéraire, 1891, p. 60). Stéphane Mallarmé's words offer an illuminating point of departure for the present work by Berthe Morisot, L'Allée du Jardin à Mézy, executed in 1891. A close friend of Morisot and the author of the preface to the artist's seminal posthumous exhibition at Galerie Durand-Ruel in 1896, in which the present work was included, Mallarmé understood the power of suggestion to reside precisely in what is left unresolved: in the space between what is seen and what is imagined.

Morisot's path to Impressionism was unusual. Born into a cultivated bourgeois family, she received a serious artistic education with her sister Edma, studying under Joseph Guichard before turning to landscape painting with Camille Corot. Her encounter with Édouard Manet in 1868 proved decisive. Their friendship, and her marriage in 1874 to his brother Eugène, brought her into the centre of the circle that would become the Impressionist movement. She exhibited at seven of the group's eight exhibitions between 1874 and 1886, establishing herself as one of its original practitioners.

Throughout her career, Morisot remained deeply committed to the principles of Impressionism, while the circumstances of her life inevitably shaped the ways in which she practised it. Following the birth of her daughter Julie in 1878, works on paper assumed an increasingly important place in her practice, offering a flexibility suited to the rhythms of family life. As Delphine Montalant observes, 'Until 1879, the year following Julie's birth, [...] Berthe had devoted herself to oil painting; it was after this date that the preference for watercolour clearly emerged. Her duties as a mother obliged her to concentrate on this more flexible, rapid technique, allowing her to express herself with greater ease and a freedom which was new to her. [...] For Christmas 1889, Julie received a box of coloured pencils as a gift, which prompted Berthe to experiment with them. Once again, the artist's work evolved thanks to her daughter: from this date onward drawing became crucial to her work' (D. Montalant in A. Clairet, D. Montalant & Y. Rouart, Berthe Morisot 1841-1895, Catalogue raisonné de l'oeuvre peint, Montolivet, 1997, pp. 16-17). Executed in pastel on paper at this moment in her career, L'Allée du Jardin à Mézy is a particularly eloquent example of this evolution: the immediacy of the medium becomes inseparable from the immediacy of the experience it records.

Morisot's stays in Mézy, at the house she rented with her family in 1890 and 1891, provided an ideal setting for this increasingly fluid practice. The garden offered all the essential conditions of Impressionist painting—light in constant flux, shifting colour, movement and direct observation of nature—within the intimate world of the home. Morisot was repeatedly drawn to such spaces of transition: gardens, balconies, verandas, windows and winter gardens, where inside and outside meet. The garden at Mézy might therefore be understood as a modern, secular hortus conclusus: an enclosed space of privacy and retreat, yet also a threshold through which the changing world of light and atmosphere enters.

Her choice of subject also reflects the particular circumstances of a woman of her social position. The boulevards, cafés, railway stations and other public spaces that provided subjects for her male contemporaries were less readily accessible to a respectable bourgeois woman. Yet the garden was not simply a retreat from modern life, nor should Morisot's choice of subject be understood as a limitation. Rather, it offered a space in which the private and the natural could meet, allowing her to pursue the same fundamental Impressionist concerns with light, movement and perception.

Claude Monet also painted his own garden in Le Jardin de Monet à Vétheuil (1881), with a sunlit path leading through luxuriant planting towards the house. At first glance, the two works share a very similar subject and compositional structure; yet Monet's path leads the viewer clearly through the garden towards the house, while Morisot's curves away into the foliage, drawing the viewer into the vegetation rather than towards a fixed destination. Her path disappears beneath the trees and loses itself among the foliage; there is no conventional vanishing point and no fixed position from which the scene can be surveyed.

This quality is particularly striking when considered alongside Pierre-Auguste Renoir's Sentier dans le bois, painted circa 1874–1877. Renoir places a barely suggested figure in the lower centre of the composition, partially absorbed into the luxuriant vegetation and its enveloping atmosphere. Morisot removes the figure altogether. Where Renoir places a figure within the landscape, Morisot places the viewer there, surrounded by the swirling movement of the foliage. The curved path is echoed in the handling of the pastel: loose, rapid strokes sweep across the surface, with greens, blues, pinks and violets circulating through the foliage. Branches bend and leaves shimmer, while the path itself seems almost to swirl beneath the trees. With no conventional vanishing point to anchor the composition, the vegetation surrounds the viewer, pressing in from every side.

Pastel is particularly suited to this effect. Unlike oil paint, its dry, immediate application allows individual marks to remain visible, preserving the sense of movement in the artist's hand. Forms hover between definition and dissolution: a branch is suggested rather than delineated, while colour can simultaneously describe foliage, light and atmosphere. What might initially appear unfinished is therefore central to the work's expressive power. Morisot does not need to describe every leaf; she gives us enough to reconstruct the sensation of the garden ourselves. In Mallarmé's terms, the painting operates through suggestion: its meaning resides not only in what is shown, but in what the viewer is invited to imagine.

The importance of L'Allée du Jardin à Mézy is further underscored by its exceptional exhibition history. The work was included in the seminal posthumous exhibition Berthe Morisot (Madame Eugène Manet) at Galerie Durand-Ruel in Paris in 1896, appearing as no. 212. Organised by Stéphane Mallarmé, Edgar Degas, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Claude Monet, the exhibition represented the first major reassessment of Morisot's achievement following her death. Its inclusion in this landmark exhibition, organised by four of her closest artistic contemporaries and at the gallery so closely associated with the promotion of Impressionism, places the present work at a particularly significant moment in the early history of Morisot's critical reception. The work was also exhibited in Berthe Morisot, Impressionist at the National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C., in 1987, the landmark retrospective that played a major role in the renewed recognition of Morisot's position within the history of Impressionism.

The sustained presence of L'Allée du Jardin à Mézy in these important exhibitions is testament to the particular significance of the work within Morisot's oeuvre. It is easy to understand why: her mastery of pastel allows the Impressionist garden to emerge not through exhaustive description, but through fragments of colour, flickering strokes and shifting passages of light, as foliage dissolves into atmosphere. In place of description, Morisot offers suggestion; in place of a fixed prospect, immersion. The Impressionist garden ceases to be simply something seen: it becomes something felt.

With the Ka paintings of 1980, Bridget Riley gave the stripe a new chromatic intensity. After a decade of increasingly complex curves and interlocking forms, the vertical band returned as a vehicle of remarkable expressive power. Blue, turquoise, ochre, brick red, black and white are brought into precise and often startling conjunctions, their relationships continually altering the appearance of the surface. The palette was seeded by Riley's journey through Egypt the previous winter, yet nothing in these paintings is descriptive. Colour is absorbed, transformed and reconstituted within the exacting logic of her abstraction. In Ka 4, the disciplined sequence of vertical bands generates an extraordinary sense of movement: colours advance and recede, intensify and dissolve as they encounter one another. An apparent order gives way to a surface in perpetual visual flux.

In the winter of 1979–80, while travelling to Japan for the final stage of a British Council touring retrospective, Riley spent several weeks in Egypt, visiting Cairo, the Nile Valley and the ancient tombs of Luxor and the Valley of the Kings. She was struck by the intensity and persistence of the colours encountered there: blue and turquoise set against ochre, brick red, black and white, recurring across objects and painted surfaces that had endured for millennia. These combinations remained with her after her return to London, where they were reconstructed through memory. The process was one of transformation rather than transcription. Egypt provided a chromatic vocabulary, which Riley absorbed into the very different language of her own abstraction.
The new palette emerged from the chromatic investigations of the preceding decade. Throughout the 1970s, Riley had explored relationships between colour and form through curves, diagonals and interlocking structures. Her return to oil brought a new density to the surface, allowing the heightened hues to achieve a saturation commensurate with their intensity. At the same time, the stripe, largely absent from her work since the late 1960s, returned as a newly charged structural device. Its vertical regularity established a rigorous framework capable of containing an unusually concentrated palette. The restraint of the format became the condition for chromatic freedom.

Blue and turquoise establish the dominant register of Ka 4, punctuated by warmer passages of ochre and brick red, while black and white sharpen the intervals between them. Each colour modifies those beside it, altering its apparent weight, temperature and intensity. A narrow band may suddenly assume prominence before receding into the sequence; another, initially subdued, gathers force through juxtaposition. The physical immobility of the stripes heightens the sensation of change. Across the surface, colours shimmer, advance and recede, their apparent relationships continually adjusting while the underlying sequence remains fixed. Stability and instability are held in precise equilibrium.

The painting is the product of an exceptionally disciplined process. Riley worked through gouache studies and collages, testing sequences and proportions before arriving at the final arrangement. Colour was considered in relation to the complete structure, each adjustment capable of altering the balance of the whole. Yet none of this deliberation is apparent in the finished work. The studies, revisions and calculations have been subsumed into an image of extraordinary clarity, in which the complexity of the construction is experienced rather than displayed. Its apparent inevitability is the result of sustained refinement.

The Ka series marks a significant development in Riley's practice, bringing the intellectual rigour of her earlier optical investigations into a more concentrated chromatic language. The restricted palette produces a remarkable range of effects, while the repetitive structure of the stripe becomes a means of differentiation rather than sameness. The paintings extend rather than abandon the formal investigations of the preceding decade, translating them into a more concentrated vocabulary of colour and perception. The works that followed would develop increasingly complex chromatic relationships; the Ka paintings retain the freshness of their first articulation.

The title introduces a further connection with Riley's Egyptian experience. In ancient Egyptian belief, the ka was understood as a vital essence or spiritual force, an aspect of the individual that survived beyond the physical body. Riley did not conceive her titles as literal keys to interpretation, and Ka 4 makes no attempt to represent an Egyptian subject. The word nevertheless resonates with the painting's origins. The Egyptian source has passed from the visible world into memory and from memory into colour. Egypt is present not as imagery, but as a transformed and elusive presence within the chromatic atmosphere of the work. Riley's response to Egypt was therefore one of assimilation. The colours she encountered entered a practice concerned not with representation but with the mechanics and instability of vision. An external experience became an internal system: ancient colour became material for a radically contemporary abstraction, while the stripe provided the architecture through which it could be ordered and released. By the time it reaches the finished canvas, the original source has almost entirely disappeared, yet its presence remains perceptible in the unusual intensity and harmony of the palette.

In Ka 4, these elements are brought together with exceptional poise. The vertical bands retain their exact positions while seeming to shimmer, recede and reassert themselves; the colours remain rigorously ordered while continually altering one another's appearance. Geometry becomes sensation, and repetition becomes a vehicle for variation. The stripe is no longer simply a compositional device but the structure through which colour acquires an almost incandescent force. At the threshold of a new decade, Riley found within one of the most elementary forms in her vocabulary an expansive means of expression. Ka 4 stands as a particularly assured embodiment of this development.

Executed in 2006, Untitled is a striking example of Günther Förg's celebrated 'Gitterbilder', or 'Grid Paintings', in which the ordered vocabulary of modernist geometry is transformed into something instinctive, physical and emphatically painterly. Across the surface, a dense lattice of black, blue, green, ochre, orange and red strokes accumulate and disperses, alternately obscuring and revealing the luminous passages beneath. Rather than functioning as a fixed geometric armature, Förg's grid remains in perpetual motion: lines overlap, falter, double back and intersect with an apparent spontaneity that belies the sophistication of the composition.

The spatial tension of the present work is particularly compelling. At its centre, an expansive field of yellow and acid green opens into the picture plane, surrounded by increasingly congested passages of vertical and horizontal marks. Darker lines appear to advance and recede simultaneously, creating a fluctuating sense of depth in which no single plane remains entirely stable. Towards the lower right, the grid fractures into a dramatic fan of dark, gestural strokes, introducing a pronounced sense of acceleration and directional movement. This passage disrupts the more rectilinear structure elsewhere in the composition, establishing a rhythm between constraint and release. The result is an image that continually shifts between enclosure and openness, structure and movement.

Förg's engagement with the grid was closely connected to his longstanding fascination with architecture and the visual language of twentieth-century Modernism. Architecture offered him a vocabulary of proportion, repetition and structure, but also a means of exploring how an apparently rational system might be translated into an inherently subjective medium. In Untitled, the grid evokes the framework of a modernist façade, the mullions of a window or perhaps the fragmented structure of an urban landscape. Yet these associations remain deliberately open. Förg does not seek to reproduce architecture; instead, he translates its underlying logic into an energetic and distinctly painterly form.

This tension between rational structure and individual gesture is fundamental to the 'Gitterbilder'. The grid traditionally suggests order, stability and rationality, while Förg's execution continually unsettles these qualities. His lines are neither mechanically straight nor evenly spaced; they vary in pressure, width and intensity, sometimes appearing almost hurriedly drawn, elsewhere becoming dense and heavily worked. Intersections accumulate across the surface, creating moments of visual congestion that are balanced by areas in which the underlying colour is allowed to breathe. The grid consequently becomes less a prescribed system than a record of movement, continually made and remade by the artist's hand.

The material presence of the painting is equally important. Förg's use of acrylic allows the colour to retain a particular luminosity, while successive layers of translucent green, yellow and blue establish a shifting ground beneath the more emphatic linear marks. Earlier gestures remain partially visible, giving the surface a sense of excavation and depth. Colour does not simply sit behind the grid; it appears to press through it, competing with the darker marks for prominence. The painting therefore operates on several levels at once: as an immediately legible abstract composition, as an accumulation of individual gestures and as an investigation into the relationship between surface and spatial illusion.

By 2006, Förg had developed the grid into a highly fluid and expansive pictorial vocabulary. The present work demonstrates the maturity of this language, balancing formal restraint with a palpable sense of improvisation. Its vitality lies precisely in the tension between the system that governs the composition and the gestures that continually disrupt it. The grid becomes at once framework and gesture, screen and window: a device for organising the picture and the means by which Förg continually unsettles it.

Ultimately, Untitled exemplifies Förg's distinctive ability to reconcile the intellectual legacy of Modernism with the immediacy of gestural painting. Its architectural references provide an underlying order, while its layered colour, irregular intersections and physical evidence of the artist's hand introduce a sense of instability and movement. Geometry becomes gesture; structure becomes space; and the grid itself becomes a dynamic field in which colour, surface and depth remain in constant negotiation.

Among the most enduring images to emerge from Banksy's early practice, Laugh Now is a quintessential expression of the visual language through which the artist transformed the conventions of street art into a powerful form of contemporary cultural commentary. Conceived at the beginning of the new millennium, the image of the stooping chimpanzee carrying a sandwich board inscribed 'Laugh now, but one day we'll be in charge' distils Banksy's characteristic combination of graphic economy, irreverent wit and pointed social observation. Yet its significance extends beyond the immediacy of its provocation. The figure's apparent subservience is placed in tension with the declaration it carries, transforming an image of submission into one of latent authority. In this reversal lies much of the enduring power of Laugh Now: a deceptively simple image becomes a meditation on hierarchy, power and the instability of established conventions.

Animals occupy a central position within Banksy's imagery, functioning as surrogates through which human behaviour and systems of authority can be viewed from an oblique perspective. Alongside the rat, the chimpanzee became one of his most recognisable protagonists, particularly suited to his interest in the boundaries between civilisation and instinct. In Laugh Now, the inversion is especially acute. The creature conventionally positioned below man within the evolutionary hierarchy is granted both a voice and the prospect of eventual dominance. The deadpan delivery is quintessentially Banksy: humour provides an immediate point of entry, while the underlying proposition is considerably more unsettling. The viewer is invited to recognise the absurdity of the situation while simultaneously questioning the assumptions upon which conventional hierarchies depend.

The importance of the motif within Banksy's early oeuvre was reinforced by its prominent public manifestation in 2002, when the Ocean Rooms nightclub on Morley Street in Brighton commissioned the artist to create a monumental, six-metre-long mural depicting a procession of chimpanzees carrying the now-iconic placards. The commission marked a significant stage in the development of the image, establishing the chimpanzee and its message within the public realm on an imposing scale. The motif subsequently reappeared across Banksy's paintings and editions, becoming firmly embedded within his repertoire. The present work, dated 2001, is particularly compelling in this context, predating the Brighton commission and capturing the image at a formative moment in its development.

Executed in acrylic and spray paint, the work retains the immediacy of Banksy's street-based methodology while translating it into the more enduring medium of canvas. The chimpanzee occupies the centre of the composition with monumental simplicity, its dark silhouette sharply delineated against an expansive pale green ground. The white placard interrupts the otherwise monochromatic figure with its deliberately old-fashioned lettering, creating a stark visual and conceptual contrast. By eliminating any surrounding narrative or architectural setting, Banksy concentrates attention entirely upon the figure and its message. The result is emblematic rather than descriptive: the chimpanzee becomes an autonomous symbol whose meaning is carried through posture, silhouette and text.

This economy of means is fundamental to Banksy's practice, in which stencil and spray paint operate as both technique and recognisable aesthetic idiom. Developed within the conditions of the public realm, the stencil enabled the artist to produce images rapidly while retaining a striking degree of graphic precision. In Laugh Now, that method is transferred to canvas without losing its original immediacy. Slight irregularities in the sprayed passages preserve the physical character of the street, while the controlled composition and square format confer upon the image the concentrated presence of a self-contained painting. The work consequently occupies a compelling space between Banksy's ephemeral interventions and his more enduring studio practice.

At the heart of the image is a carefully sustained contradiction. The chimpanzee appears defeated, its head lowered and shoulders weighted beneath the placard, yet the words it carries anticipate a reversal of precisely this condition. Humour and menace are consequently held in equilibrium. The phrase can be read as a satirical comment on authority and social hierarchy, but it also carries a broader suggestion of the instability of any established order. Banksy does not resolve the tension between comedy and threat; instead, he allows the two to coexist within an image of extraordinary economy. This ambiguity is central to the work's sophistication, enabling it to remain immediately legible while resisting a single interpretation.

Within Banksy's oeuvre, Laugh Now occupies a particularly important position. Few of his early images combine such instant recognition with such conceptual clarity, and fewer still demonstrate so effectively his ability to compress a complex idea into a single, unforgettable visual gesture. The chimpanzee would become one of the artist's defining protagonists, while the image itself evolved from an early motif into one of the most recognisable compositions associated with his practice. The present canvas is especially significant for the way it captures that image at an early and formative stage, retaining the raw immediacy of Banksy's street practice while possessing the scale, materiality and permanence of a singular work on canvas.

Ultimately, Laugh Now demonstrates the force of Banksy's art: the ability to make an image appear instantly simple while allowing its implications to unfold long after the initial encounter. The stooping chimpanzee is at once comic, vulnerable and quietly defiant, while its placard proposes a future in which the established order may no longer hold. It is this tension between humour and unease, simplicity and ambiguity, that has secured Laugh Now a defining place within Banksy's early oeuvre.

Fernando Botero's Homme à Table is a striking expression of the singular pictorial language that made the Colombian artist one of the most recognisable figures in post-war art. An imposing man, impeccably dressed and seated behind a table, confronts the viewer with a remarkable combination of presence and restraint. Set against a saturated pink wall, his expansive form dominates the compressed interior, while the carefully orchestrated arrangement of furniture, objects and architectural details establishes a world governed by Botero's distinctive sense of scale. Familiar at first glance yet unmistakably transformed, the scene demonstrates his ability to turn an ordinary moment into an image of extraordinary theatricality and visual authority.

The sitter is quintessentially Boterian. His enlarged body occupies the narrow confines of the room with almost sculptural solidity, his broad shoulders and substantial limbs contrasting with his small, meticulously modelled head and composed expression. The vivid wall provides a dramatic counterpoint to the brown of his jacket and blue neckerchief, while turquoise accents and warm wooden tones animate the surrounding space. Colour and form are not merely descriptive here; they constitute the architecture of the composition. The figure does not simply inhabit the room but determines its peculiar proportions, his physical presence making the surrounding space appear simultaneously intimate and monumental.

For Botero, this expansion of form was never simply a device of caricature. From the late 1950s onwards, he developed an increasingly distilled approach to enlarged and simplified forms, in which proportion itself became expressive. His figures and objects acquire an extraordinary physical presence precisely because they depart from naturalistic scale. Volume, sensuality and distortion became the foundations of a pictorial universe governed by its own coherent logic. In Homme à Table, that logic is apparent not only in the sitter but throughout the composition: every object, interval and architectural element has been subjected to the same deliberate transformation.

This highly individual language was rooted in Botero's deep engagement with the history of Western art. His travels in Europe during the 1950s, particularly his encounters with the Old Masters in Spain and Italy, were formative. He absorbed the monumentality of Renaissance painting, the serene equilibrium of Piero della Francesca, the precision of early Italian forms and the intensity of Spanish colour and character. Yet his achievement lay in transformation rather than imitation. He brought the compositional authority and gravity of traditional painting into dialogue with a distinctly modern sensibility, creating a language that was at once historical and entirely his own.

That dialogue is especially compelling in Homme à Table. The frontal pose and stillness of the sitter recall the formal presence of traditional portraiture, while the compressed perspective and exaggerated proportions make the image unmistakably Botero's. A small, framed picture, an open doorway and a selection of carefully positioned domestic objects heighten the scene's sense of artifice. Nothing appears incidental. Figure and setting have been subjected to the same rigorous formal treatment, producing an environment in which scale, colour and geometry work in concert. As in Botero's many depictions of interiors, family groups, musicians and social gatherings, the ordinary is transformed into something highly composed and almost ceremonial. Here, the table establishes a strong horizontal division across the composition, while the restricted architecture intensifies the sitter's physical presence. There is humour in the distortion of scale, but it is balanced by an unmistakable dignity: the figure is neither mocked nor sentimentalised but possesses the quiet self-assurance of someone entirely at home within Botero's carefully constructed world.

Executed in 1996, the present work belongs to a period of considerable confidence in Botero's career. By the mid-1990s, the visual vocabulary that had established his international reputation was fully formed, enabling him to explore its possibilities with the assurance of a mature artist. The work brings together several of the enduring concerns of his practice: the relationship between figure and space, the expressive potential of distortion, the authority of traditional genres and the tension between humour and seriousness. Rather than pursuing stylistic reinvention, Botero continued to refine and expand a language that had become entirely his own.

This equilibrium between humour, grandeur and formal discipline lies at the heart of Botero's achievement. At a moment when abstraction, Pop Art and conceptual practices dominated much of the international avant-garde, he pursued figuration with remarkable independence. His paintings remained deeply engaged with the history of representation while developing an instantly recognisable language of their own. Whether depicting Colombian life, the circus, bullfighting, religious subjects or the rituals of everyday existence, Botero subjected his themes to a rigorous transformation, making the familiar strange, monumental and newly theatrical. Homme à Table distils this approach with particular clarity, taking an apparently simple domestic encounter and giving it the weight and authority of a formal tableau.

That singular vision carried far beyond his Colombian origins. Over the course of a seven-decade career, Botero became one of the most internationally celebrated Latin American artists of the twentieth century, earning the affectionate appellation of "the Maestro" for the authority and consistency with which he developed his distinctive artistic language. His paintings and drawings entered important museum and private collections, while his monumental sculptures became landmarks in public spaces around the world. Yet the immediacy of his work has never depended upon simplicity alone. Beneath the apparent directness of his compositions lies a sophisticated engagement with proportion, perspective, colour and the history of Western representation. Homme à Table rewards precisely this duality: its visual language is immediately legible, yet its carefully calibrated distortions reveal a far more considered formal structure.

Following Botero's death in 2023, the extraordinary consistency of this achievement has acquired renewed historical resonance. He spent his career refining a vision established early in his practice while continually finding new subjects through which to test it. The result was more than a recognisable style: Botero created an entire pictorial universe, governed by a distinctive conception of space, scale and form, and populated by figures whose quiet grandeur has become one of the defining images of modern Latin American art.

Within this achievement, Homme à Table is an assured example of Botero's mature practice. Its saturated palette, concentrated composition and imposing protagonist bring together the qualities that have made his work so enduringly compelling: immediate visual impact, formal sophistication and an unmistakable artistic identity. The sitter's steady gaze, the richly coloured interior and the deliberate manipulation of scale transform an apparently simple domestic scene into something theatrical, enigmatic and timeless. Painted at a moment of complete artistic confidence, Homme à Table exemplifies Botero's extraordinary ability to make the everyday monumental, and to make that transformation entirely his own.

'She sways, crosses, winds her way along, adorned with every imaginable kind of hat, through the long red-draped promenades [...] beneath the whitish glow of the gas jets.' Émile Zola's description of the crowd at the Folies Bergère in 1882 evokes a world of movement, artificial illumination and social encounter: a crowd that was itself as much a spectacle as the entertainment taking place before it (E. Zola, 'Les Folies Bergère', in Cronaca Bizantina, 1 April 1882). It is precisely this atmosphere that Jean-Louis Forain captures in the present work, Sortie des Folies Bergère, executed around 1895. Rather than depicting the performers, he makes the audience his subject: a shifting assembly of men and women whose clothes, gestures and glances create a theatre of their own.

Opened in 1869, the Folies Bergère was one of Paris's great music halls, combining songs, dances, comedy and spectacular stage attractions. Yet it was also a place to see and be seen. Spectators could circulate, drink and converse, making the audience itself part of the entertainment. By the 1890s, the Folies Bergère had become emblematic of Belle Époque Paris, where fashion, pleasure, commerce and flirtation converged.

Forain was exceptionally attuned to this world. His friendship with Edgar Degas, whose pioneering depictions of the theatre, ballet and their surrounding social rituals had helped define a new vision of modern Parisian life, was formative; Forain himself began exploring the Folies Bergère as a subject in the late 1870s. He returned repeatedly to its bars, foyers and audiences, less interested in recording entertainment than in observing the relationships enacted around it: between men and women, or spectator and spectacle.

The composition is animated by a succession of groups and encounters. A sea of top hats dominates the crowd, their dark silhouettes forming an almost continuous horizontal band against which the women stand out vividly. Although men considerably outnumber women, it is the women who are more individually characterised. Forain gives them colour, gesture and physiognomic presence, while many of the men remain deliberately anonymous, their faces obscured beneath brims or absorbed into the dark mass of the crowd. 

The woman in the green dress on the left appears to look directly towards the elegantly dressed man on the right, whose face and top hat distinguish him from the surrounding crowd. Her attention establishes an immediate, though deliberately unexplained, connection between them. Elsewhere, at the threshold of the doorway, another man appears to look discreetly towards the two women gathered on the right. Forain thus constructs a series of intersecting gazes without ever resolving them into a narrative. We are left to speculate: is this courtship, recognition or curiosity?

These two women on the right are particularly striking in this respect. Framed by the two doorways and surrounded by men, they are visually and socially enclosed within the scene. Forain isolates them as objects of attention while simultaneously suggesting their awareness of being watched. The tension recalls Manet's Un bar aux Folies Bergère of 1882. Manet isolates his barmaid behind the counter, complicating the relationship between woman, male customer and viewer through the reflection in the mirror. Forain disperses a similar psychological tension throughout his crowd. Here there is no single transaction but a multitude of possible encounters: figures may be looking, being looked at, waiting to be approached or deliberately avoiding another's gaze. 

Amid this shifting play of glances, the central woman stands with striking assurance. Wearing a long dark skirt, white shirt, narrow tie and bowler hat, she stands apart from the elaborately dressed women around her. She is not engaged in any obvious exchange; instead, she leans casually against the wall, her posture relaxed and almost nonchalant.

Her appearance introduces a subtle disruption of conventional gender codes. The bowler, shirt and tie were strongly associated with male urban dress, yet Forain's figure is not simply a woman dressed as a man. Her long skirt retains a distinctly feminine silhouette; rather, she has appropriated selected elements of masculine dress and, with them, something of the freedom and authority traditionally associated with the male spectator.

For women at the time, masculine-coded accessories such as the bowler hat, tie or tailored jacket could signal modernity and independence. Such fashions were associated with the 'amazone', the term for a woman who rode astride and whose practical riding dress incorporated elements of masculine clothing; by the 1890s, these elements had begun to enter everyday fashion. At the Folies Bergère, a woman appearing alone in the 'promenoir' - the area where spectators could circulate, socialise and observe both the performance and one another - could adopt the visual language of male fashion and claim a similar freedom of movement and observation. Forain's central figure may therefore be understood as an embodiment of a new female presence in the public spaces of Belle Époque Paris: self-possessed, mobile and conspicuously unwilling to remain merely the object of another's gaze. Within the Folies Bergère, she is at once participant and observer, feminine yet subtly masculine in appearance, and conspicuously at ease in a public world traditionally dominated by men.

Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec's Au Moulin Rouge (1892-1895), painted around the same time, offers a parallel vision of Parisian nightlife. Like Forain, Lautrec transforms the entertainment venue into a theatre of social observation, placing the viewer almost within the crowd. Yet Forain's figures are less overtly theatrical. His spectators are caught in fleeting moments of attention, while the central woman possesses an enigmatic independence that resists easy classification. Lautrec's world is one of performers and personalities; Forain's is one of social roles being subtly assumed, exchanged and disrupted.

Forain's pastel and gouache technique heightens the sense of transience. Broad passages of red, brown and black dissolve into flashes of turquoise, green, blue and white; faces emerge briefly from the darkness, while hats and garments are established with economical, almost instantaneous strokes. The crowd seems to move before our eyes. The medium itself becomes an extension of the subject: fluid, atmospheric and suggestive of the fleeting impressions of modern life.

In Sortie des Folies Bergère, Forain transforms the music hall into a sophisticated study of Belle Époque society. The Folies Bergère is not merely its setting but its subject; the crowd becomes the theatre without a stage, in which the boundaries between spectator and spectacle remain tantalisingly fluid.

BÃ¤ume am Walchensee 
signed and dated 'Lovis Corinth 1921' (upper left)

19.9 x 28cm (7 13/16 x 11in).
Painted in 1921

Provenance
Dr Gustav Kirstein Collection, Leipzig (probably acquired directly from the artist).
Adolf Wüster, Munich.
Private collection, Germany.
Private collection, UK (by descent from the above in 1988).

Literature
C. Berend-Corinth, Lovis Corinth, Die Gemälde, Werkverzeichnis, Munich, 1992, no. 831 (illustrated p. 780).

Painted in 1921, Bäume am Walchensee belongs to a defining period in Lovis Corinth's late career, when the Alpine landscape of the Walchensee became an enduring source of artistic inspiration. In these works, the artist found a subject through which colour, gesture and the experience of nature could be brought into remarkable accord. Trees, mountains, water and sky cease to be merely descriptive elements and instead seem to participate in the shifting atmosphere of the landscape itself. In the present work, painted on an intimate panel, Corinth draws the viewer into the dense vegetation surrounding the lake, transforming a secluded corner of the Walchensee into an image of extraordinary vitality.

Lovis Corinth first travelled with his family to the small village of Urfeld, on the northern shore of the Walchensee, in the summer of 1918. The encounter proved decisive. The artist was immediately captivated by the beauty of his surroundings and by the particular character of the mountains, light and air. The following year, his wife, Charlotte Berend-Corinth, commissioned the construction of a house on the hillside overlooking the village, which would later become known as Haus Petermann. From its terrace, Corinth commanded an expansive view across the lake towards the surrounding mountains, a panorama to which he would return repeatedly in paintings, watercolours and drawings.

The Walchensee came to occupy a central place in Corinth's late work. Its constantly changing appearance seems to have fascinated him. Writing in 1921, the very year in which the present work was painted, Corinth described how, 'The lake changes in mysterious colours and moods. At one moment it flashes like an emerald, at another it becomes blue like a sapphire' (L. Corinth, 'Am Walchensee', 1921, reproduced in W. Timm, ed., Die Bilder vom Walchensee. Vision und Realität, Bremen, 1986, pp. 23-24). This sensitivity to nature as something mutable rather than fixed lies at the heart of Bäume am Walchensee. Corinth does not attempt to describe every branch or leaf; instead, he evokes the sensation of being surrounded by nature, with its flickering light, dense foliage and glimpses of brilliant colour.

Across the small surface of the panel, paint is worked with striking freedom. Deep greens, blacks and earthen browns establish the shadowed mass of the trees, through which passages of turquoise and blue suggest the lake and sky beyond. Touches of yellow and creamy white flare against the darker ground, catching the light like leaves momentarily illuminated through the canopy. The tree trunks at the centre are built from vigorous vertical strokes, while the surrounding foliage dissolves into a restless network of marks. The paint shifts between passages of thick, tactile application and areas of greater openness, where rapid sweeps of the brush allow the support beneath to remain visible. The landscape appears simultaneously substantial and elusive, as though Corinth were attempting to seize an impression before the light changed again.

An interesting parallel can be drawn with Walchensee mit Lärche, also painted in 1921 and today in the Alte Nationalgalerie, Berlin. There, a tall larch tree rises prominently in the foreground, set against the broad expanse of the lake and distant mountains. While Walchensee mit Lärche opens outward towards the panorama of the water and Alps, Bäume am Walchensee turns inward. The trees themselves become the subject, almost obscuring the landscape beyond. Yet the two works share the same animated handling of paint and the same sense of a natural world alive with movement. Significantly, both date from 1921, a year in which Corinth was honoured with a doctorate by the University of Königsberg and the Nationalgalerie's Kronprinzenpalais mounted a major retrospective of his work.

Despite its modest dimensions, Bäume am Walchensee possesses an exceptional concentration of energy. Rather than presenting the Walchensee as a distant prospect, Corinth places the viewer within the landscape itself: among the trunks, shadows and flashes of foliage, with the luminous blue of the lake glimpsed between them. Nature is not simply observed here but experienced. In Corinth's restless strokes, light breaks through the darkness, colour flickers across the surface, and the familiar landscape of the Walchensee is transformed into something intimate and profoundly alive.

M. Harvey, The Bronzes of Rembrandt Bugatti (1885-1916), Ascot, 1979, no. 22 (plaster version illustrated p. 34; titled 'Small cat').
